title: What should you ask first in a private equity case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a private equity case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Ask first what return the fund needs and over how long, because a private equity case is judged against that hurdle, not against whether the company is good. The trap is having no view on the exit: who buys the business in a few years, at what price, and what is left for the fund once debt is repaid.
body:
The first question to ask

What return does the fund need, and over how long does it plan to hold the business?

Private equity cases are close cousins of acquisition cases, with a sharper focus on returns and a planned sale a few years later. A fund targeting 2.5x its money over five years needs a very different plan from one happy with 2x. The answer gives you the bar every option must clear. Ask, too, how the deal will be financed: how much is equity and how much is debt.

How to build your structure

  • Market: size and growth, margins, barriers to entry.
  • Company: position against peers, performance, management team.
  • Value creation: revenue growth, margin improvement, add-on acquisitions.
  • Deal: entry price and how much debt the business can safely carry.
  • Exit and returns: likely buyers, exit price, money multiple and yearly return against the fund's target.

The full tree is in the private equity framework.

Worked example: why the exit matters

A fund buys a company with $10M of EBITDA at 10x, so it pays $100M. It puts in $40M of equity and borrows $60M. Over five years EBITDA grows to $14M and the business pays down $20M of debt, leaving $40M.

StepCalculationResult
Exit value$14M × 10$140M
Equity at exit$140M − $40M debt$100M
Money multiple$100M ÷ $40M2.5x
Yearly return2.5^(1/5) − 1about 20%

The $60M gain on equity has two sources: $40M from EBITDA growth ($4M × 10) and $20M from paying down debt. (This ignores fees, tax and any cash paid out before exit.)

Now stress-test the exit. If buyers only pay 8x in five years, exit value is $14M × 8 = $112M, equity is $72M, and the multiple drops to 1.8x, about 12.5% a year. To still reach 2.5x at 8x, the fund would need EBITDA of $17.5M at exit ($140M ÷ 8), 25% more than the plan. The same company, bought at the same price, is a good or poor deal depending on the exit. For the maths behind yearly returns, see compound growth and CAGR.

The trap most people fall into

No exit thinking. Candidates analyse the market and the company well, then stop. A fund only makes money when it sells, so the answer must cover who will buy, at what multiple, and what that leaves for equity after debt.

Weak: "It's a strong business in a growing market, so the fund should buy it."
Strong: "At a 10x exit the deal returns 2.5x, which meets the target. But at 8x it falls to 1.8x, so I'd only invest if we're confident in at least 10x, or can grow EBITDA to $17.5M."

Two prompts to try

A fund is considering buying a regional chain of veterinary clinics.

Show the answer
  • Market: growth in pet ownership and spend per pet; how fragmented the market is.
  • Company: clinic profits, vet retention, prices against local rivals.
  • Value creation: buy and integrate smaller clinics; shared purchasing; add services such as diagnostics.
  • Exit: likely buyers (larger groups, other funds) and the multiple they pay.

Where to start: value creation through add-ons. In a fragmented market, buying small clinics cheaply and selling the larger group at a higher multiple can drive much of the return.

The trap: forgetting that vets can leave, taking their clients with them.

A fund is offered a fast-growing software company at 20x EBITDA.

Show the answer
  • Growth: how fast revenue and EBITDA grow, and how long that can last.
  • Quality of revenue: recurring share, net revenue retention, customer concentration.
  • Deal: how much debt a business like this can carry.
  • Exit: what multiple it can sell for, and how much EBITDA growth is needed if that multiple is lower.

Where to start: exit multiple. At 20x entry, a fall to 15x at exit wipes out a quarter of the value.

The trap: assuming the high entry multiple will hold.
